stories.headline: Diljit Dosanjh's 'Satluj' pulled from OTT: The CBFC row and takedown explained
stories.what: Diljit Dosanjh's film 'Satluj' has been embroiled in a significant controversy involving the Central Board of Film Certification and an OTT takedown, sparking a nationwide debate on censorship and creative freedom. The film, which deals with sensitive subject matter, was removed from its streaming platform amid a dispute with the CBFC. The controversy has drawn sharp reactions from across the film industry and public figures. It is being compared to several other Indian OTT titles that have faced similar regulatory or legal troubles.
stories.lens: The 'Satluj' takedown raises a pointed question every Indian streamer faces: who ultimately decides what you can watch at home, and on what grounds?
stories.article:
Diljit Dosanjh's film 'Satluj' has been pulled from its OTT platform following a dispute with the Central Board of Film Certification, triggering one of the sharpest censorship debates in Indian entertainment in recent memory. The controversy centres on a conflict between the film's certification status and its streaming availability, with the takedown raising urgent questions about the regulatory framework governing OTT content in India.

The film's removal has drawn immediate and vocal reactions from across the film fraternity. Actor Ranvir Shorey described the OTT takedown as 'utterly disappointing', while comedian Kunal Kamra invoked the name of slain human rights activist Jaswant Singh Khalra — whose story the film reportedly touches upon — saying 'Jaswant Singh Khalra abducted again' in a pointed critique of the CBFC's role. The backlash signals how the controversy has moved well beyond a procedural dispute into the territory of free expression and historical memory.

The Times of India's detailed explainer traces the sequence of events from the initial CBFC row to the eventual OTT removal, providing context for what appears to be an escalating stand-off between the film's producers and the certification body. Hindustan Times, meanwhile, contextualised the episode by listing four other Indian OTT films and shows that have previously run into regulatory or legal trouble, suggesting that 'Satluj' is part of a broader pattern of content disputes on streaming platforms.

The episode arrives at a moment of heightened scrutiny of OTT regulation in India, with the government having extended CBFC-adjacent oversight to streaming content. For Dosanjh, who commands one of the most devoted fan followings in Indian popular culture, the takedown of 'Satluj' is likely to intensify both public sympathy and pressure on the authorities to clarify the grounds for the film's removal.
key_facts: Diljit Dosanjh's film 'Satluj' removed from OTT platform
Dispute involves the CBFC (Central Board of Film Certification)
Actor Ranvir Shorey called the takedown 'utterly disappointing'
Kunal Kamra criticised CBFC, invoking Jaswant Singh Khalra
At least four other Indian OTT titles have faced similar troubles

stories.headline: Review: Alia Bhatt's 'Alpha' called a crowd-pleaser shaped by the 'Dhurandhar' moment
stories.what: A critical review in The Indian Express argues that Alia Bhatt's action film 'Alpha' appears to 'go rogue' in a bid to capitalise on what the reviewer terms the 'post-Dhurandhar landscape' — a reference to the wave of patriotic, high-octane Bollywood action films energised by Ranveer Singh and Aditya Dhar's project. The piece suggests that 'Alpha' has shaped its tone and content to pander to this trending genre rather than chart its own course. The review adds to a broader conversation about whether Bollywood is entering a new cycle of action-patriotism filmmaking.
stories.lens: The review signals that Alia Bhatt's pivot to full-throttle action cinema is being read as a calculated industry move, reflecting how a single buzzy film can rapidly reshape what Bollywood greenlit.
stories.article:
Alia Bhatt's 'Alpha' has arrived in the crosshairs of a pointed critical review, with The Indian Express arguing that the film deliberately recalibrates itself to exploit what it calls the 'post-Dhurandhar landscape' of big-budget Bollywood action cinema. The suggestion is that 'Alpha' has sacrificed a degree of originality to position itself within a commercially lucrative genre trend.

The review's framing is significant: 'Dhurandhar', the forthcoming collaboration between director Aditya Dhar and Ranveer Singh, has apparently already cast a shadow over Bollywood's production choices even before its release. That a film not yet in theatres can be cited as a defining aesthetic reference point underlines the extraordinary anticipation surrounding the Dhar-Singh project.

For Alia Bhatt, 'Alpha' represents a major genre shift — away from the character-driven dramas that made her reputation and towards the kind of muscular, high-stakes action that has dominated the Indian box office in recent years. Whether that is a savvy career move or a concession to formula is precisely the debate the review appears designed to provoke.

The broader question raised by the piece is whether Bollywood is cycling into a new phase of genre consolidation, where patriotic action films set the commercial agenda and other films reconfigure themselves accordingly. For audiences deciding whether to watch 'Alpha', the review's central claim — that the film is reacting to a trend rather than setting one — will be a meaningful consideration.
key_facts: 'Alpha' stars Alia Bhatt in an action-led role
Review argues the film panders to a 'post-Dhurandhar' action-film trend
'Dhurandhar' is directed by Aditya Dhar and stars Ranveer Singh
